title: Replication
scopeHtml:
Scope: leader-follower, multi-leader, leaderless, quorum math, replication lag fixes.

Scope: leader-follower, multi-leader, leaderless, quorum math, replication lag fixes.

notes.title: Why replicate data
notes.html:
Replication means keeping copies of the same data on several machines. You do it for three reasons: survive a machine dying (availability), serve more reads (throughput), and put data near users (latency).

It does not help with data that is too big for one machine; that is sharding (next file). Every replication design answers one question: when a write happens, who accepts it, and who must confirm before we say "done"?

Worked example. A Postgres primary does 2,000 writes/s and 18,000 reads/s. One box handles about 20,000 total, so it is at the edge. Add 2 replicas for reads: primary keeps 2,000 writes, each replica serves 9,000 reads. Capacity is now roughly 3x for reads, 1x for writes.

Industry examples. Instagram and GitHub run Postgres/MySQL with many read replicas. Amazon Aurora keeps 6 copies of storage across 3 availability zones.

Everyday analogy. Photocopying an important document and keeping copies in different houses: a fire in one house does not lose it, but now you must keep all copies up to date.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying replication solves write scaling. It does not; every replica still applies every write.
  • Forgetting the cost: N copies means N times the storage and replication bandwidth.

notes.title: Leader-follower replication
notes.html:
One node (the leader, also called primary or master) accepts all writes. Followers (replicas) copy its changes and serve reads.

The leader writes each change to a log (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog). Followers stream that log and replay it in the same order. Same order is the whole point: it guarantees followers converge to the same state.

Choices:

  • Synchronous: leader waits for the follower to confirm before acknowledging the client. No data loss, but one slow follower stalls writes.
  • Asynchronous: leader acknowledges immediately. Fast, but if the leader dies before the log reaches a follower, those writes are lost.
  • Semi-sync (the usual answer): wait for exactly one follower, the rest are async. Postgres: synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (r1, r2)'. MySQL has semi-sync plugin.

Worked example. Same-region follower round trip is about 1 ms; a cross-region one is about 80 ms. Fully sync across regions means every write costs at least 80 ms, so teams use sync in-region and async cross-region.

Failover. When the leader dies, promote the most up-to-date follower. Steps: detect (heartbeat timeout, for example 10 s), choose, repoint clients, make the old leader a follower when it returns. Danger: split brain, where the old leader comes back and still thinks it is the boss. Fix with fencing (kill the old node, lease/epoch numbers). Tools: Patroni for Postgres, Orchestrator for MySQL, Redis Sentinel.

Decision gravity. Choosing async is reversible by config but the data-loss window is accepted at design time. Choosing a single leader is chosen for simplicity (no write conflicts). It breaks when write volume exceeds one machine or when users are far from the leader. Switching later to multi-leader or sharding is a one-way door.

Industry examples. Postgres streaming replication, MySQL at Facebook/Uber (async with GTID), MongoDB replica sets (election among members using a Raft-like protocol), Redis replication (async by default).

Everyday analogy. One teacher writes on the board and students copy it into notebooks in the same order. Only the teacher writes, so notebooks never disagree, but if the teacher faints mid-sentence, someone has to take the chalk.

Common interview traps.

  • Promoting an async follower without admitting that acknowledged writes may be lost.
  • Ignoring split brain.
  • Saying "automatic failover is easy". Wrong detection (a slow network, not a dead node) causes needless failovers.

notes.title: Replication lag and how to hide it
notes.html:
Replication lag is the delay between a write on the leader and it appearing on a follower. Normally milliseconds; under load, a big transaction or a network blip, seconds or minutes.

Symptoms users see:

  • Read-your-writes violation: you post a comment, refresh, it is gone (the read hit a stale replica).
  • Monotonic read violation: you see a new post, refresh, it vanishes (second read hit a more lagged replica).
  • Causality violation: you see an answer before the question.

Fixes, cheapest first:

  1. Read from the leader right after a write (for example for 5 s, or for the user's own profile).
  2. Sticky replica per user (hash user id to a replica) so reads never go backwards in time.
  3. Track a position token: after a write, return the LSN/GTID; the next read goes only to a replica that has reached it (Postgres pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()).
  4. Route by lag: drop replicas lagging more than, say, 2 s from the pool.
-- Postgres: how far behind is this replica?
SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS lag;

Worked example. A 2 GB bulk UPDATE on the leader replays serially on a replica (single-threaded in older MySQL), so lag jumps from 50 ms to 90 s while followers are busy. Metric: seconds_behind_master or replay_lag. Fix: batch updates in 10k-row chunks, use parallel replication.

Industry examples. Facebook's early architecture famously used a "recently wrote" cookie to pin users to the master for about 20 seconds. Many Rails apps use a similar primary-for-a-while trick.

Everyday analogy. You mail a letter and ask the post office if it was received; the clerk at a branch that has not updated yet says "no". Ask the original branch instead.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing "just use sync replication" without the latency and availability cost.
  • Not mentioning which guarantee you need (read-your-writes vs monotonic vs consistent prefix).

notes.title: Multi-leader replication
notes.html:
Several nodes accept writes, and each forwards its changes to the others. Typical use: one leader per region (Mumbai, Frankfurt, Virginia) so every user writes to a nearby node, and each region keeps working if the links between them break.

The price is write conflicts: two users edit the same row in different regions at the same moment, and both writes were accepted locally.

Conflict handling:

  • Avoid: route all writes for one record to the same region (home region of the user).
  • Last write wins (LWW): highest timestamp wins. Simple, silently loses data, and clocks drift.
  • Merge: keep both values (siblings) or use CRDTs (counters, sets that merge mathematically).
  • Custom resolver/app logic: ask the user, or apply business rules.

Real systems use all-to-all links (each leader sends to every other), which avoids one broken link stopping the flow but can reorder events.

Worked example. Two offices edit a calendar event title. Mumbai writes "Standup" at 10:00:00.100, Virginia writes "Sync" at 10:00:00.090 (clock skewed 20 ms behind). LWW keeps "Standup" even if Virginia's edit was actually later in real time. This is why important systems prefer version vectors over timestamps.

Decision gravity. Chosen when write latency across regions or offline operation matters more than simplicity. Alternatives: single leader plus follower reads, or sharding by region. It breaks when conflicts are frequent or data has invariants (account balance cannot go negative). Hard to undo, because data created with conflicts has already been merged lossily.

Industry examples. Google Docs style collaboration (operational transform/CRDT), CouchDB, MySQL Group Replication in multi-primary mode, Cassandra across datacenters (leaderless but similar effect), Active-active setups like AWS DynamoDB global tables (LWW by default).

Everyday analogy. Two people editing their own copy of a shared shopping list on separate phones; when they meet, the lists must be merged and someone bought milk twice.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing multi-leader just for "high availability" when a single leader with failover suffices.
  • Using auto-increment ids, unique constraints or counters across leaders without handling conflicts.

notes.title: Leaderless replication and quorum math
notes.html:
No leader: the client (or a coordinator) sends each write to several replicas and each read to several replicas, and compares answers. This is the Dynamo design (Amazon Dynamo paper, then Cassandra, Riak, ScyllaDB).

Parameters: N replicas hold each key, W must acknowledge a write, R must answer a read.

Rule: if W + R > N, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one node, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write (assuming no concurrent writes and no sloppy quorum).

N W R Property
3 2 2 Balanced, tolerates 1 node down for both
3 3 1 Fast reads, writes fail if any node down
3 1 3 Fast writes, reads slow
3 1 1 W+R=2, not greater than 3, can read stale, max availability

Worked example. N=3, W=2, R=2. Write v2 reaches A and B; C is down. A read asks B and C: B returns v2, C returns v1 (old). The coordinator picks the newer version by timestamp/version and does a read repair, writing v2 to C. Background anti-entropy using Merkle trees repairs keys nobody reads.

Other tools:

  • Hinted handoff: if C is down, another node stores the write with a hint and gives it to C when it returns.
  • Sloppy quorum: accept writes on any N healthy nodes even if not the home nodes, trading consistency for availability. W+R>N no longer guarantees fresh reads.
  • Cassandra consistency levels: ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, ALL. Typical production: LOCAL_QUORUM for both reads and writes with RF=3 per datacenter.
-- cqlsh
CONSISTENCY LOCAL_QUORUM;
INSERT INTO orders (id, status) VALUES (42, 'PAID');

Edge cases where quorum still gives stale reads. Concurrent write and read, a write that failed partway (applied on some nodes but reported failure), a node restored from stale backup, clock skew with LWW.

Decision gravity. Chosen for availability and no failover pause (no leader to elect). Alternative: consensus-based (Raft in etcd, Spanner), which gives strong consistency at higher latency. It breaks for workloads needing transactions or strict ordering. Switching later is a one-way door because the data model (wide rows, no joins) changes.

Industry examples. Amazon DynamoDB (originally Dynamo), Apple runs huge Cassandra clusters (reported over 100k nodes), Discord used Cassandra for messages then moved to ScyllaDB, Netflix uses Cassandra for viewing history.

Everyday analogy. A decision needs signatures from 2 of 3 managers; any 2 managers always share at least one person who knows the latest decision.

Common interview traps.

  • Stating W+R>N guarantees strong consistency. It does not under sloppy quorum or concurrent writes.
  • Mixing up N (copies) with the cluster size.
  • Forgetting that a quorum write needs W replicas up; with N=3, W=3 is less available than a single leader.

notes.title: Choosing a replication style
notes.html:
Simple decision flow:

  1. Need transactions, joins, strict consistency, one region? Single leader, semi-sync follower in the same region, async elsewhere.
  2. Users spread over continents and writes must be local, conflicts tolerable? Multi-leader with home-region routing.
  3. Massive write volume, always-on, simple key-value access, eventual consistency OK? Leaderless with quorums.
  4. Need strong consistency and automatic failover across zones? Consensus replication (Raft/Paxos: etcd, CockroachDB, Spanner, MongoDB majority writes).

Worked example. A payments ledger: leader-follower with sync replica in another AZ (RPO=0), ROUTE reads for balances to leader. A chat history store: Cassandra RF=3, LOCAL_QUORUM, since a message appearing a few ms late is fine.

Everyday analogy. One editor-in-chief (leader), several regional editors (multi-leader), or a committee voting (quorum).

Common interview traps.

  • Picking a style without stating the consistency requirement and RPO/RTO targets.
  • Forgetting cross-region latency numbers (Mumbai to Virginia about 200 ms RTT).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Replication = copies for availability, read throughput and latency. It does not scale writes.
  • Leader-follower: one writer, ordered log; sync vs async vs semi-sync trades latency for data-loss risk. Beware split brain on failover.
  • Replication lag causes stale reads: fix with read-your-writes (pin to leader), monotonic reads (sticky replica), LSN tokens, lag-based routing.
  • Multi-leader: local writes everywhere, but conflicts; prefer avoiding them, else merge or LWW (lossy).
  • Leaderless: N, W, R; W+R>N gives overlap but not magic; read repair, hinted handoff, anti-entropy.
  • Pick by consistency need, geography and write volume; leader changes are one-way doors.

questions.promptHtml: Our primary database is at 90% CPU. A teammate says "add two replicas and we are done." When is that right and when is it wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know replication scales reads and availability, not writes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Replication keeps copies of the same data on several machines. It helps with three things: surviving a machine failure, serving more reads, and putting data near users. It does not scale writes, because every replica still applies every write. So if the CPU is from reads, replicas help. If it is from writes, they do not, and I would look at sharding, batching or a bigger box.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
First split the load: how many reads and writes per second? Example: 2,000 writes/s and 18,000 reads/s on a box that tops out near 20,000 total. Add 2 replicas: the primary keeps 2,000 writes, each replica serves about 9,000 reads. Read capacity roughly triples, write capacity stays 1x. In fact replicas add work for the primary (it must ship the log to each one), so write headroom shrinks slightly.

Before: Primary  = 2,000 W + 18,000 R  (at the edge)
After : Primary  = 2,000 W (+ log shipping)
        Replica1 = 2,000 W (replay) + 9,000 R
        Replica2 = 2,000 W (replay) + 9,000 R

Costs: N copies means N times storage and replication bandwidth, plus the new problem of stale reads (replication lag).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying replication fixes write scaling.
  • Forgetting replicas also replay every write, so a write-heavy workload leaves them just as busy.
  • Forgetting that reads from replicas can be stale.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a replica a backup? -> No. A bad DELETE replicates instantly. You still need point-in-time backups.
  2. What do you do if the writes are the problem? -> Batch, remove indexes you do not need, move to bigger hardware, then shard.
  3. How do you stop replicas serving stale data to the user who just wrote? -> Read-your-writes routing (pin to the leader for a short time, or LSN tokens).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "add replicas for scale". The senior answer first measures read vs write mix, shows the capacity math, names the stale-read cost and says replicas are not backups.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams add replicas to a write-bound primary, see no change and then learn replay is the same work as the original write.

questions.promptHtml: Explain synchronous, asynchronous and semi-synchronous replication, and what actually happens to your data when the leader dies in each case.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you can state the RPO of each mode and know failover is the dangerous part.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In sync mode the leader waits for a follower before acknowledging the client, so no acknowledged write is lost, but a slow follower stalls writes. In async mode the leader acknowledges right away, so it is fast but writes not yet shipped are lost if the leader dies. Semi-sync waits for exactly one follower and leaves the rest async, which is the usual compromise. On failover I promote the most up-to-date follower and must fence the old leader to prevent split brain.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The leader writes every change to an ordered log (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog). Followers replay it in the same order, which guarantees they converge.

Mode Client ack when Data loss on leader crash Write latency
Async leader wrote its log possible, the unshipped tail lowest
Sync (all) all followers confirmed none worst follower, and one down follower blocks writes
Semi-sync 1 follower confirmed none, if that follower survives one round trip

Failover steps: detect (heartbeat timeout, for example 10 s), pick the follower with the highest log position, repoint clients, demote the old leader when it returns. Split brain happens when the old leader is only partitioned, not dead, and both accept writes. Fix with fencing: STONITH, lease or epoch numbers, so a node with an old epoch is rejected.

-- Postgres: wait for any 1 of 2 named standbys
ALTER SYSTEM SET synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (r1, r2)';

Same-region round trip is about 1 ms, cross-region about 80 ms, so teams use sync in-region and async across regions.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Promoting an async follower without admitting acknowledged writes may be lost.
  • Ignoring split brain.
  • Believing automatic failover is trivial; a slow network can look like a dead node and cause needless failovers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not sync to all followers? -> Availability of writes drops with every extra follower; one slow node stalls everyone.
  2. How do you pick the new leader? -> Highest replayed log position (LSN/GTID); tools like Patroni or Orchestrator do it.
  3. What if the old leader had writes the new leader never got? -> Those diverge; rewind or rebuild the old node, and report the lost writes to the business.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists the three modes. The senior states RPO and RTO for each, explains fencing and says what the business must be told about lost writes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An async cluster failed over during a network blip; 4 seconds of orders existed only on the old leader.

questions.contextHtml:
A comments feature writes to the primary and reads from a pool of 3 replicas. Support tickets: "I posted a comment, the page reloaded and my comment is gone, then it appears after a few seconds." Replica lag dashboard shows a steady 200 to 400 ms. The code:

Comment c = commentRepo.save(newComment);          // goes to primary
return redirect("/post/" + c.getPostId());
// later, in the GET handler:
List<Comment> list = readPool.pick().findByPost(postId);   // random replica
val c = commentRepo.save(newComment)               // goes to primary
return redirect("/post/${c.postId}")
// later, in the GET handler:
val list = readPool.pick().findByPost(postId)      // random replica
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug, and how do you fix it without sending all traffic back to the primary?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make replication synchronous." That adds write latency and availability risk, and still does not cover every replica.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the user see only their own missing comment, or others too (own only means read-your-writes)? Is lag always under 1 s? Is there a login session I can hang state on?
  2. Immediate mitigation: For 5 to 10 seconds after a write, route that user's reads to the primary.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) read-your-writes violation: redirect read hits a replica that is 300 ms behind; b) caching layer serving the old list; c) replica outage (ruled out by lag metric).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log the replica id and pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() on the read; compare with the LSN returned after the write. Check CDN or page cache headers.
  5. Root cause: The redirect arrives in about 50 ms, much less than the 200 to 400 ms lag, so the read beats the replication.
  6. Fix: Short term: set a "wrote recently" cookie with a timestamp and read from the primary for 5 s. Long term: return the commit LSN to the session and have the router pick only replicas that have replayed it.
  7. Prevention: Integration test that writes then reads through the router; alert when the share of primary-routed reads exceeds a threshold.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make all replicas sync; I would not read from the primary always, since that erases the scaling benefit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if a different user reloads and sees the comment vanish after having seen it? -> Monotonic read violation; use a sticky replica per user.
  • What if the user has two devices? -> The cookie is per device; use a server-side token keyed by user id.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team pinned reads for 60 s "to be safe" and quietly sent 70% of reads to the primary. Pinning only the writer for 5 s cut that to 4%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests full sync replication, or does not identify the race.
  • Hire: names read-your-writes and fixes with a time-bounded primary read.
  • Strong hire: adds LSN tokens, monotonic reads, and measures the primary read share.

questions.contextHtml:
Tuesday 02:10. A nightly job runs UPDATE orders SET archived = true WHERE created_at < now() - interval '1 year' touching 40M rows (about 2 GB of WAL). At 02:14 the alert fires: replica lag 90 s and climbing. The customer app reads order status from replicas; support reports "order shows Pending but I paid". Primary CPU is 35%, replica CPU is 100% on a single core.

 replay_lag    | write_lag | flush_lag
---------------+-----------+----------
 00:01:32      | 00:00:00.2| 00:00:00.4

Network shows no loss.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and what do you do now and next?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Network problem, restart the replicas." Restarting makes it worse since replay resumes from the same point. Write and flush lag are tiny, so the network is fine.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which DB and version (parallel replay available)? Is the job safe to stop? Which reads must be fresh?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause the job (the rows already committed stay). Route critical reads (order status after payment) to the primary. Remove the lagging replica from the pool if lag exceeds 5 s.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) one huge transaction replayed by a single apply process (matches: write/flush lag low, replay lag high, one core at 100%); b) replica disk I/O saturated; c) replica query conflicts blocking replay (Postgres max_standby_streaming_delay); d) network (ruled out).
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_stat_replication on the primary, pg_stat_activity and top on the replica, iostat -x, and check pg_stat_database_conflicts.
  5. Root cause: The primary executes the update with its own concurrency, but the standby replays the WAL mostly serially, so a 2 GB burst takes minutes to apply while new queries see old data.
  6. Fix: Short term: stop the job, wait for lag to drain. Long term: rewrite the job in 10k-row batches with a short sleep between them and a lag check (pause if lag > 2 s). On MySQL enable parallel replication (replica_parallel_workers).
  7. Prevention: Alert on replay lag (not just receive lag), run bulk jobs through a throttled batch helper, route reads by lag.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not kill the replica to resync (hours of rebuild). Smaller batches make the job take longer, which is fine at night.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the job cannot be paused? -> Move readers to the primary until lag drains; accept the extra load.
  • How would you bound staleness for the product? -> Lag-based routing, drop replicas above 2 s.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A backfill ran at 03:00 and lag reached 40 minutes; the cache then refilled from stale replicas and served wrong balances until midday. The cache TTL, not the DB, was the longer outage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the network, restarts things.
  • Hire: identifies serial replay of a large transaction and batches the job.
  • Strong hire: separates write, flush and replay lag, adds lag-aware routing and throttled jobs.

questions.contextHtml: A payments ledger runs a Postgres primary in Mumbai (ap-south-1a). The CTO asks for RPO = 0 across a regional disaster and wants a second region in Singapore (about 60 ms RTT) as a standby. The ledger does 1,500 writes/s at peak, each write transaction currently commits in about 3 ms. The SLO is p99 write latency under 50 ms.
questions.promptHtml: Do you configure the Singapore standby as synchronous? What would you propose?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, sync everywhere for zero loss" (ignores that commit becomes at least 60 ms and breaks the SLO) or "async, it is fine" (ignores RPO = 0).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is RPO = 0 required for a whole region loss or just a zone loss? What is the RTO? Is the latency SLO on the user-facing path or can the ledger write be off the critical path?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design). I would state the math: sync cross-region commit is at least 60 ms plus fsync, so p99 around 70 ms, above the 50 ms SLO. 1,500 writes/s at 70 ms needs about 105 concurrent commits, which is manageable, but the latency SLO fails.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (options): a) sync standby in a second AZ in Mumbai (1 ms) for RPO=0 for zone loss, async to Singapore for region loss (RPO of seconds); b) sync to Singapore, relax SLO; c) consensus store (Raft quorum across 3 regions).
  4. How I'd verify each: Measure real RTT with ping/mtr, benchmark with pgbench and synchronous_commit = remote_apply vs on.
  5. Root cause of the tension: Physics: the speed of light sets a floor on cross-region commit.
  6. Fix: Recommend (a), with synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (az_b)' and an async Singapore standby. For the region-loss RPO, ask the business whether seconds of loss is acceptable or whether the ledger must pay the 60 ms.
  7. Prevention: Monitor lag to Singapore, alert at RPO breach (for example 5 s), run a failover drill each quarter.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Option (b) is a decision about the business: this is reversible by config, but the accepted loss window must be signed off. I would not use sync to a far region without telling the SLO owner.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the AZ standby goes down? -> With ANY 1 of 2 AZ standbys, writes continue; with one only, writes block, so run two.
  • What if they insist on RPO=0 for the region? -> Put it on the ledger write path only and accept about 70 ms, or use a Raft-based store like CockroachDB/Spanner.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team turned on cross-region sync "temporarily" for an audit and checkout p99 doubled; nobody remembered the setting for three weeks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks one extreme without numbers.
  • Hire: computes latency floor, proposes in-region sync plus cross-region async.
  • Strong hire: separates zone loss from region loss, asks for the business RPO, notes it is a config-reversible choice with a one-way risk acceptance.

questions.contextHtml:
A MySQL cluster (1 primary, 2 replicas, async, orchestrator-managed) in one region. At 14:03 a switch flaps; the orchestrator cannot reach the primary for 12 s and promotes replica-2. The old primary is fine, just partitioned from the orchestrator, and app servers in rack B still reach it. At 14:05 the network heals. Now two nodes accept writes.

14:03:12 orchestrator: primary db-1 unreachable (heartbeat timeout 10s)
14:03:14 orchestrator: promoting db-2 (gtid 7f3a:1-884213)
14:03:15 app-b: connected to db-1 (read_only=OFF)
14:05:20 app-a/app-b: 1,100 INSERT conflicts ... duplicate key on orders.id
questions.promptHtml: What do you do in the first 15 minutes, and how do you stop this recurring?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Point everyone at db-2 and move on." That throws away the writes that only reached db-1 and never reconciles anything.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many writes landed on each node since 14:03? Are ids generated per node (auto-increment) or globally? Which writes are money-related?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fence db-1 now: SET GLOBAL super_read_only=ON or stop it at the network/instance level. Point all apps to db-2 via the one service name. Freeze the batch jobs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) false-positive failure detection (matches: node is healthy); b) clients caching the old primary address; c) no fence in the promotion script.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare GTID sets (gtid_executed) on both; mysqlbinlog on db-1 for transactions not in db-2; app connection logs for stale endpoints.
  5. Root cause: Failover without fencing. Promotion happened while the old leader was still alive and writable, so the system had two leaders (split brain), and 10 s of heartbeat loss was treated as death.
  6. Fix: Short term: extract the divergent transactions from db-1 binlog, replay or manually merge the legitimate ones, rebuild db-1 as a replica of db-2. Long term: fence before promote (power/network fence or a lease), require two independent observers to agree, set the old primary read_only on any demotion hint, add a semi-sync ACK so db-2 has the tail.
  7. Prevention: Raise detection to consensus of several probes, use a service discovery that refuses a leader without the current epoch, run game days with partitions.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not auto-merge by timestamps, and I would not just wipe db-1 before extracting its transactions, since there may be paid orders only there.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How would semi-sync have changed this? -> The promoted replica would hold all acknowledged writes, so less divergence; it does not prevent split brain.
  • What if the clients are in an app that caches DNS for 60 s? -> Use a proxy with a leader check or set short TTL plus client retry on read-only errors.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An orchestrated failover during a switch upgrade left 380 orders on the old node; finance reconciled them by hand over two days. The permanent fix was a fence step in the promotion hook.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: does not recognise split brain.
  • Hire: fences the old node and compares GTIDs before deciding.
  • Strong hire: preserves and reconciles divergent writes, explains the fencing/lease design and tests with partition drills.

questions.promptHtml: In a Dynamo-style store with N, W and R, why does W + R > N matter, and what does it not guarantee?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Quorums are the core of leaderless designs; many candidates overstate the guarantee.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: N is the number of replicas holding a key, W is how many must acknowledge a write and R how many must answer a read. If W + R > N, any read set shares at least one node with any write set, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write. It is not a strong-consistency guarantee: concurrent writes, sloppy quorums, partially failed writes and clock-skewed last-write-wins can all still give stale or lost data.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
With N=3, W=2, R=2: a write to A and B, a read from B and C. B is in both, so the coordinator sees v2 from B and v1 from C, picks the newer and does a read repair to C. Pigeonhole: two groups of sizes W and R out of N overlap when W + R > N.

N W R Result
3 2 2 balanced; one node can be down
3 3 1 fast reads; any node down fails writes
3 1 3 fast writes; slow reads
3 1 1 W+R = 2, stale reads possible, max availability

Repair mechanisms: read repair (fix during reads), hinted handoff (a neighbour holds writes for a down node), anti-entropy with Merkle trees (background compare). Sloppy quorum accepts writes on any N healthy nodes, which keeps availability but breaks the overlap guarantee. Cassandra exposes this as consistency levels: ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, ALL.

-- cqlsh
CONSISTENCY LOCAL_QUORUM;
INSERT INTO orders (id, status) VALUES (42, 'PAID');

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying W + R > N means linearizable.
  • Confusing N with the cluster size.
  • Using W = N, which is less available than a single leader.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if a write fails after reaching only 1 of 3 nodes? -> It may still be visible later; the client sees an error but the data exists, so retries must be idempotent.
  2. Why LOCAL_QUORUM? -> Avoids cross-datacenter latency; quorum is within the local DC.
  3. How does LWW lose data? -> Two concurrent writes, the one with the lower (maybe skewed) timestamp is discarded silently.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer recites the inequality. The senior lists the failure modes where it does not hold and chooses the consistency level per query.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team used ONE for reads and writes "for speed" and saw users reading their old address after an update.

questions.promptHtml: When is multi-leader replication justified, and how do you handle write conflicts?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who pick it for "availability" from those who understand its cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I use multi-leader when writes must be local in several regions or must work offline, and a cross-region round trip on each write is not acceptable. The cost is conflicts: two regions accept different writes to the same record. I first avoid conflicts by routing a record's writes to its home region, then use a merge (CRDT, siblings) or custom resolution, and treat last-write-wins as lossy.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each region has a leader that replicates asynchronously to the others (usually all-to-all, so a broken link does not stop flow, though events can arrive out of order).

Conflict strategies:

  • Avoid: pin a user or tenant to a home region.
  • LWW: the highest timestamp wins; simple, silently drops writes, depends on clocks.
  • Merge: CRDT counters and sets merge mathematically; siblings are shown to the app/user.
  • Version vectors detect concurrency honestly (A and B are concurrent versus A happened before B).
Mumbai  10:00:00.100  title = "Standup"
Virginia 10:00:00.090 title = "Sync"      (clock 20 ms behind, actually later)
LWW keeps "Standup" -> Virginia's edit silently lost

Things that break across leaders: auto-increment ids, unique constraints, counters, and any invariant such as "balance never negative".

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Choosing multi-leader just for HA when single leader plus failover is enough.
  • Auto-increment keys and unique constraints across leaders.
  • Trusting wall clocks for ordering.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Alternatives for global users? -> Single leader with follower reads, or shard by region with a home region per user.
  2. Is it reversible? -> Hard; data merged lossily cannot be unmerged.
  3. How do you make an inventory counter safe? -> Not with multi-leader LWW; keep the invariant in a single home region or use escrow/reservation per region.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "active-active for high availability". The senior says conflict avoidance comes first, names the invariants that cannot tolerate it, and flags it as a one-way door.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An active-active profile service lost address updates under LWW because a region's clock drifted; fixed by home-region routing.

questions.contextHtml:
A Cassandra cluster, RF=3, one DC. Reads and writes use LOCAL_QUORUM (QUORUM = 2). A node (n3) goes down at 09:00 for 4 hours of maintenance. At 11:30 a user changes their email; a support agent immediately reads the old email once, then the new one on retry. The team says "quorum should have prevented this". Logs:

09:00 n3 DOWN
11:30:01.120 write email=new@x.com  acks: n1, n2  (ok)
11:30:01.310 read  CL=LOCAL_QUORUM  contacted: n1, n3?  -> old@x.com

n3 was restarted at 11:29 and is still replaying hints.
questions.promptHtml: Explain how this read returned the old value, and what you would change.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Cassandra is eventually consistent, ignore it." That does not explain why quorum was not enough, or whether it is a bug.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the write acknowledged with CL=LOCAL_QUORUM? Which replicas did the read contact? Any sloppy quorum or ANY? Was this a one-off?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Nothing urgent; run repair if a node was down longer than the hint window (max_hint_window, 3 hours by default, verify).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) the read set included n3 and n1/n2 and the coordinator returned a stale value because of a timestamp tie or a failed write; b) n3 returned the old value and the coordinator did not reconcile; c) clock skew affecting LWW; d) a write at a lower CL.
  4. How I'd verify each: TRACING ON in cqlsh to see replicas and timestamps, nodetool status, nodetool tpstats for hints, compare WRITETIME(email) on each replica at CL=ONE per node.
  5. Root cause: W=2 + R=2 > N=3 should overlap. If the read really got n1's answer, it should return new. So either the write timestamp was older than the stored one (clock skew, so LWW kept old on one node) or the read used a lower CL. The mechanism: quorum overlap guarantees only that a node with the newest write is asked; the winner is still picked by timestamp.
  6. Fix: Short term: sync NTP/chrony, check WRITETIME. Long term: use client-side timestamps carefully, or lightweight transactions (IF conditions) for rows that need strict ordering.
  7. Prevention: Monitor clock offset (<10 ms alert), run nodetool repair regularly (within gc_grace_seconds), enforce CL in driver config.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not move to ALL (any node down fails requests), and I would not call it acceptable without checking the timestamps.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the write used sloppy quorum or hinted a non-replica? -> The overlap guarantee is gone; reads at QUORUM can miss it until the hint is delivered.
  • What does LWT cost? -> Paxos rounds, several round trips; use sparingly.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A customer's "new password" write lost to an old one because one app host's clock was 4 s ahead; quorum was fine, the timestamps were not.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: shrugs it off as eventual consistency.
  • Hire: explains overlap and checks tracing and timestamps.
  • Strong hire: identifies clock skew/LWW, names LWT as a targeted fix and monitors skew.

questions.contextHtml: A product manager says: "We are launching in Mumbai, Frankfurt and Virginia next quarter. Users in all three must see fast writes and the app must survive a region outage. Let's go active-active." Today you have one Postgres primary in Virginia with 3 replicas. Traffic: 30M DAU, 8,000 writes/s peak, 85% of users stay in one region, data includes profiles, orders and a wallet balance.
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond to this requirement, and what would you propose?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Sure, set up multi-master Postgres in each region." No questions about invariants, conflicts or which data actually needs local writes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "fast" mean (p99 target)? Which writes are latency-sensitive (profile edits, or just orders)? What RTO/RPO for a region outage? Can a user write from two regions (travel)? Is the wallet balance allowed to be eventually consistent?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not a mitigation scenario. I would first measure: Mumbai to Virginia is about 200 ms RTT, so one write is at least 200 ms; that is the problem we are solving.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (options): a) home-region sharding: each user has a home region and a regional primary, with async backup to a second region; b) multi-leader with merge for profile data, single home for wallet; c) a global consensus DB (Spanner/CockroachDB) at higher commit latency and cost.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype one data class; measure cross-region write latency, count conflicting writes in a replay of production traffic (same row written in two regions within the lag window).
  5. Root cause of the tension: Local writes in many places mean concurrent writes to one item; consistency and latency trade off.
  6. Fix (proposal): Start with (a): 85% of users stay in one region, so route by home region and make orders/wallet single-writer there; replicate async to another region for DR (RPO of seconds, agreed with the business). Use LWW or CRDTs only for low-risk fields like profile.
  7. Prevention: Per-table conflict policy in the design doc, conflict counter metric, region failover game days.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Full multi-leader is a one-way door; I would not use it for balances or unique-constraint data (usernames, orders ids), and I would not use auto-increment ids across regions (use region-prefixed or UUID ids).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A user travels from Mumbai to Frankfurt? -> Reads local; writes still go to the home region (extra latency) or migrate home after a threshold.
  • Home region down? -> Promote the DR replica; accept the RPO, communicate to the business.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch plan "active-active everywhere" was reduced to per-region ownership after a replay showed 0.3% of rows would have conflicted daily, all of them money-related.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts the requirement as stated.
  • Hire: asks about conflicts, invariants and latency targets.
  • Strong hire: proposes per-data-class strategy with numbers, names the one-way door and a measurement plan.

questions.contextHtml: You own two new services. (A) A payments ledger: 3,000 writes/s, balances must never be wrong, single region, RPO = 0, RTO < 2 min. (B) A chat message history: 120,000 writes/s, reads by conversation, a message appearing 100 ms late is fine, must stay writable when a node or AZ is down, 3 AZs.
questions.promptHtml: What replication style and settings would you pick for each, and why?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use the same Postgres cluster for both" or "NoSQL for both because it scales". Neither states consistency needs.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: (A) Do reads of balances need to be fresh? Cross-region DR? (B) Ordering within a conversation only? Retention? Read pattern?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (options): (A) single-leader Postgres with a sync standby in another AZ or a Raft-based store; (B) leaderless with RF=3 LOCAL_QUORUM (Cassandra/Scylla), partition key = conversation id.
  4. How I'd verify each: Load test: (A) pgbench with synchronous_commit on, check p99 commit under 20 ms; (B) a cassandra-stress run at 120k writes/s with RF=3 (about 360k replica writes/s across the cluster) and kill a node mid-test.
  5. Root cause of the choice: (A) invariants and transactions require one ordering authority; (B) volume and availability matter more than strict ordering and joins are absent.
  6. Fix (settings): (A) ANY 1 sync standby in another AZ, balance reads go to the leader, failover via Patroni with fencing. (B) RF=3, LOCAL_QUORUM read and write, repair weekly, hinted handoff on.
  7. Prevention: Failover drill for A, node-kill drill for B, lag and hint backlog alerts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not put the ledger on eventual-consistency storage and I would not run chat on a single leader needing a failover pause. Both choices are one-way doors in data model terms.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Chat needs "unread count" exactly? -> Use a counter service or store per-user read pointer; Cassandra counters are weak, avoid.
  • Ledger must go to two regions with RPO 0? -> Consensus store or pay cross-region sync latency.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A wallet service built on a leaderless store needed a quarter-long rewrite after double spends under concurrent writes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: same tech for both without reasoning.
  • Hire: single-leader plus sync for ledger, leaderless quorum for chat.
  • Strong hire: gives settings, test plan and states the one-way door cost.

questions.contextHtml:
Last Friday a primary in an async-replicated Postgres cluster lost its disk controller at 19:41. Patroni promoted replica-1 in 38 s. Customers reported missing data: 1,240 orders accepted by the app between 19:40:57 and 19:41:03 do not exist after failover. Metrics from before the crash:

replica-1 replay_lsn lag: 6.1 MB (about 4 s of WAL at peak)
replica-2 lag: 11 MB
sync standby: none configured

Payment gateway captured payments for those orders. The VP asks for a post-incident review.
questions.promptHtml: Walk through what happened, what you would tell the business, and the corrective actions.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Bad luck with hardware." The loss was a predictable consequence of async replication and was never accepted formally.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What RPO was written down? Which writes were acked to customers? Can the old primary's disk be recovered (WAL tail)? Does the payment gateway have the records?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Try to recover the WAL from the dead primary's disk (pg_waldump / copy segments) and replay the missing orders. Rebuild from the gateway's capture list if not. Notify customers affected, refund or recreate.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: a) async commit window (about 4 s) lost on crash (matches); b) promoted the wrong replica (replica-1 had less lag, correct); c) failover bug (none, 38 s is expected).
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare the last LSN on the old primary (if readable) to the promoted replica's, check the Patroni logs for the chosen candidate, reconcile gateway captures against orders table.
  5. Root cause: Async replication with no sync standby meant the acknowledged tail only existed on the primary. The system was designed with an implicit RPO of seconds that was never agreed with the business.
  6. Fix: Short term: reconcile and compensate. Long term: semi-sync (ANY 1) to an in-region standby in another AZ; write order and payment idempotency keys so reconciliation can be automatic; outbox from the payment webhook.
  7. Prevention: Document RPO/RTO per service, alert on replication lag above the RPO, quarterly failover game days checking for lost writes.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Semi-sync costs about 1 ms per commit and reduces write availability if both standbys are down; I would not make it fully sync to every replica, and I would not blame the on-call.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Could synchronous_commit = remote_write be enough? -> It waits until the standby OS has the data, not flushed; a small loss window remains (verify exact semantics in the docs).
  • What if business refuses the 1 ms? -> Then RPO is non-zero and must be signed off.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An incident review found that nobody had ever answered "what is our RPO"; the answer, after one lost-order incident, took ten minutes and a signature.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames hardware, no business view.
  • Hire: links loss to async commit, proposes semi-sync and reconciliation.
  • Strong hire: addresses RPO ownership, recovery of the WAL tail, idempotent reconciliation and drills.
